title: Tail QoS regression — hypothesis walkthrough and hotpatch validation
content:
Summary:
On 2025-11-04 we observed a regression in customer-visible tail QoS for a subset of production traffic. P99 generation latency climbed from a steady ~210ms to peaks around 550–700ms for ~2 hours, causing SLO misses and an escalation from a key early-adopter customer. This doc captures the investigation hypothesis, evidence from profiling, the hotpatch we deployed, and validation steps to prevent recurrence.

Impact and scope:
- Affected: hosted inference pool region-us-west-2, mixed small/medium sequence workloads (avg seq len 128).
- Observable metrics: p50 unchanged, p95 rose from 220ms -> 320ms, p99 rose from 210ms -> 550–700ms. Error rates stable.
- Customer-facing: one escalation from AcmeInc reporting intermittent 5–10x slower responses on complex multi-turn chat.
- Time window: anomaly began ~2025-11-04 09:10 UTC, contained by 2025-11-04 11:30 UTC after hotpatch rollback and traffic-routing changes.

Initial signals and triage:
1) Alerts: automated SLO alert (p99 > 300ms) fired at 09:20 UTC; on-call paged and Slack channel created.
2) Correlated change set: a scheduled rollout completed the night before (2025-11-03) that introduced a scheduler tweak to fanout prioritization and a background prefix-cache repopulation routine to speed cold requests.
3) Quick checks: no network instabilities, host CPU/GPU average utilization within expected ranges, no infra-wide kernel updates.

Investigation steps and profiling evidence:
- Request trace sampling: traced slow requests end-to-end. Wall-clock breakdown showed long blocking in the local RPC queue and worker scheduler wait time (median additional 280ms on slow traces).
- CPU flame graphs (service side): increased time in mutex acquisition around the scheduler priority queue and in the background repopulation loop. Contention hotspots pointed at function fanout_enqueue() and repopulation_scheduler::tick().
- perf and system stats: context switch rate increased ~2.3x on affected hosts during incident window.
- GPU timeline (NVIDIA profiling): kernel execution times unchanged; however there were gaps between CPU->GPU submission spikes consistent with CPU-side queuing.
- Heap/GC: no notable Python GC pauses; memory trends stable.
- Log correlation: instances with highest repopulation throughput aligned with worst tail traces.

Hypothesis (summary):
The new background prefix-cache repopulation aggressively drove fanout work onto the same worker threads used for serving, causing priority inversion under certain traffic mixes. When repopulation tasks started, they saturated the scheduler's non-preemptive queue and the scheduler tweak (favoring fairness across keys) increased head-of-line blocking for short, latency-sensitive requests. The combined effect produced long FIFO waits on worker threads and dramatically increased tail latency even though average GPU utilization and kernel times were normal.

Root cause evidence mapping:
- Temporal correlation: repopulation jobs began at 09:05 and aligned with p99 spike.
- Code path: fanout_enqueue() lock hold times increased 8–12x in sampled traces when repopulation was active.
- Repro on staging: synthetic traffic that mixes small chat requests with dense repopulation workloads reproduced p99 spikes in a staging cluster when scheduler tweak enabled.

Immediate mitigations and hotpatch deployed:
1) Rollback: reverted the scheduler prioritization tweak (PR 1986) to restore pre-rollout queuing behavior. Rollback completed 09:50 UTC.
2) Throttle background repopulation: introduced a rate limit and moved repopulation work to a separate worker pool with lower scheduling priority. Hotpatch rolled at 10:05 UTC.
3) Traffic routing: temporarily drained the most affected hosts and shifted traffic to cold-standby hosts to reduce customer impact.
Result: p99 returned to ~220ms by ~11:10 UTC; customer reported improved response times and we cleared the escalation.

Hotfix validation plan (what we ran):
- Canary run: deployed to 2% of serving fleet with mix traffic for 2 hours. Monitored p50/p95/p99, context switches, mutex contention stats, and repopulation throughput.
- Synthetic stress tests: replayed production traces with added repopulation background tasks; validated that p99 stayed under 300ms across 10 runs.
- Microbench: measured lock hold times on fanout_enqueue() down to <10ms median under new worker pool config.
- Customer verification: coordinated with AcmeInc to route a subset of their traffic through canary nodes for verification.
content_continued:
Longer-term fixes and owners:
- Short-term (2w): ensure repopulation tasks run in a separate async pool with enforced CPU shares; add a soft TTL to repopulation so it backs off under high queueing. Owner: Ben Cho (eng-serving-runtime).
- Medium-term (1–2mo): redesign scheduler to support preemptible short paths and implement adaptive worker affinity that isolates latency-sensitive flows. Owner: Lena Martínez (serving scheduler).
- Observability: add a specific metric for repopulation throughput and lock hold time, plus an alert that triggers before p99 SLO breach when repopulation/backfill rate exceeds threshold. Owner: Owen Patel (observability).
- Post-deploy tests: add this traffic mix to our nightly BVT (backwards compatibility tests) to catch regressions early. Owner: eng-serving-runtime QA.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Is the current fairness policy useful for other workloads or should we make it opt-in per model class?
- Can repopulation be redesigned to use incremental async hints from the KV-store instead of batch-driven work?
- Capacity planning: if repopulation becomes common at scale, we may want a dedicated background pool per region.

Action items (concrete):
- INF-1427: implement separate worker pool and throttle (Ben) — due 2025-11-18.
- PR 1994: add metrics and alerts for repopulation throughput (Owen) — due 2025-11-13.
- Design doc: scheduler preemption options (Lena) — draft by 2025-11-25.
- BVT update: include mixed-workload trace (QA) — due 2025-11-12.

Lessons learned:
- Background maintenance work (repop/rehydration) can become a first-class source of tail latency; treat these as high-risk in rollouts.
- Small scheduler prioritization changes can interact non-linearly with background processes; always run mixed-workload stress tests before rollout.
- Observability gaps: we lacked an early signal for lock/mutex contention; adding these metrics will shorten detection time.

Appendix (short refs):
- Key traces: trace-ids 20251104-09-1921, 20251104-09-2017 (available in tracing UI).
- Staging repro recipe: run mixed_trace_repro.sh with flags --repop-rate=high --scheduler=fair.
- Hotpatch PRs: rollback PR 1986, throttle PR 1992.

If you have follow-up questions or new data (heap dumps, flamegraphs), add to the linked Slack thread or drop notes in the Confluence page linked above.
